catalog_quote: In sum, the following typological contrasts can be identified as distinguishing Sa'ban from other PKLD dialects: 1. STRESS. In PKLD and all of its known descendants other than Sa'ban stress is penultimate. In Sa'ban, as just noted, it is generally final, but may be marginally phonemic, depending upon the interpretation of extrametrical schwa in the sequences -/ieC/ and -/ueC/. [pp.260-261:] First, it retains a contrast between *a, *i and *u in prepenultimate (pretonic) syllables. ... In Kelabit dialects, including Tring, prepenultimate *a, *i and *u have merged as schwa except in the passive/perfective infix -/in/- ... [sec. 5.2.4:] One likely precondition for erosion from the left in Sa'ban was a shift from the PKLD pattern of penultimate word stress to final stress. new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Blust 2001, all Kelabit-Lun Dayeh (PKLD) descendants except Sa'ban -- a class in which he explicitly places Long Terawan Tring -- have penultimate word stress. BUT Blust's own 1971 field transcriptions of Tring (notebook RB2-003-A pp.23-27, saved) mark stress on the final syllable of every polysyllabic citation form, and Blust 2006:315 (quoted by Mortensen 2021:52) describes N. Sarawak stress as final in citation forms but penultimate in phrasal context, near-even in Kelabit/Lun Dayeh. So: penult by the author's generalization, final in his citation-form data; no Tring-specific published sentence was accessible.
new_statements.exceptions: Sa'ban (final stress, marginally phonemic with extrametrical schwa in -ieC/-ueC) is the stated exception within KLD; nothing Tring-specific.
new_statements.domain_note: The 2001 statement is a family-level typological generalization, not a description of Tring; the conflicting notebook evidence is citation forms elicited from a single speaker (George Bidui) in one session. Likely reconciliation (Blust 2006 via Mortensen): final prominence in citation forms vs penultimate in phrasal context; unverified for Tring. The Tring-specific phonology paragraph is in Blust 1984 SMJ sec. 1, not accessible online.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern data are for the Tring dialect of Long Terawan (Tutoh River, Baram, Sarawak; one speaker, George Bidui, recorded by Blust in 1971), which Blust classes as a Kelabit(-Lun Dayeh) dialect; Glottolog trin1273 / ISO tgq. Ray 1913's 'Treng' covers Balait and Tabun (and Long Pata, which Ray himself says is a Lower Baram language, not Dayic). Note the our source list lat/lon (1.335, 110.036) points to western Sarawak, far from Long Terawan (~3.9N 114.6E) -- likely a Glottolog coordinate issue, not a different language.

Long Terawan Tring is treated in the same paper as a Kelabit(-Lun Dayeh) dialect (Table 1 p.254 'LTT'; p.260-261 'In Kelabit dialects, including Tring'; p.271 Type-3 dialects 'Kelabit: Long Terawan Tring'). Sa'ban itself pp.266-267: 'Stress is normally final'. No sentence names Tring's stress specifically.

sources.note: Primary data, no prose statement: every polysyllabic Tring citation form is transcribed with the stress tick before the FINAL syllable (du'ah '2', tə'luh '3', tu'duʔ '7', pu'luʔ '10', ma'ʔit, ñi'du, kə'tət, ba'tək, tu'laŋ, bəpi'kil, səlu'bit, ləmu'lun, təma'lut, təmə'čul, etc.); no penult-stressed forms seen on pp.23-27. This conflicts on its face with Blust 2001's blanket 'penultimate' (but matches Blust 2006:315's remark, via Mortensen 2021, that N. Sarawak languages show final stress in citation forms).
